script.title: How London's Great Stink Built Its Sewers

lines: A politician fled a meeting with a handkerchief pressed to his nose.
It was Benjamin Disraeli, in London, in June 1858.
For years, London's old sewers had emptied straight into the River Thames.
Flushing toilets and a growing city poured in even more waste.
Then came a heatwave. The river dropped, and raw sewage sat on its banks.
Queen Victoria and Prince Albert tried a pleasure cruise. They turned back within minutes.
Newspapers called it the Great Stink.
Parliament soaked its curtains in lime chloride. It didn't work.
Politicians even talked about moving the government out of London.
You see, it's like a bin nobody empties.
Spray all the perfume you want. Only taking out the rubbish fixes it.
So Disraeli pushed a new law through Parliament in weeks.
It backed engineer Joseph Bazalgette's giant sewer plan.
Sloping sewers carried the waste east, beyond the city.
Pumping stations lifted sewage into higher pipes.
Londoners blamed the smell for spreading cholera.
But doctor John Snow argued cholera spread through dirty water.
Bazalgette's sewers ended the cholera outbreaks anyway, and they still serve over nine million people.

claims.claim: Disraeli left a committee room with a handkerchief applied to his nose because the smell was so bad, in June 1858.
London's ageing sewer system emptied directly into the Thames; flushing toilets and a rising population sent more water and effluent into the sewers.
In June 1858 hot, dry weather lowered the Thames and raw effluent remained on the banks.
Queen Victoria and Prince Albert attempted a pleasure cruise but returned to shore within a few minutes; the press called it the Great Stink.
Parliament's river-side curtains were soaked in lime chloride without success; moving government to Oxford or St Albans was discussed.
Disraeli tabled a bill on 15 June that passed on 2 August, favouring Bazalgette's plan.
Bazalgette's sewers sloped east to outfalls beyond the metropolitan area; pumping stations lifted sewage into higher pipes.
Cholera was believed to spread by miasma; John Snow posited water-borne transmission.
Bazalgette's work brought an end to the cholera outbreaks; his system serves a city of over nine million.

cast.bazalgette: a 39 year old Victorian engineer with thick dark mutton-chop sideburns, a long nose, a dark grey frock coat and a black cravat, 1850s
